The worn joint surfaces of the thigh bone and the shin bone in the knee are replaced with metal parts, and a plastic liner is placed between them. Sometimes the surface of the kneecap is replaced too.
The operation is most often done for severe arthritis (osteoarthritis), when pain and limited movement do not go away with treatment without surgery.
Standing up and walking with a walker usually begin early, under the supervision of a physical therapist. The ward team decides exactly when.

Fasting:

you usually need to finish a light meal at least 6 hours before anesthesia starts, and a fatty or heavy meal at least 8 hours before. Clear liquids, such as water, can usually be drunk until 2 hours before anesthesia. With some conditions, including diabetes and slow emptying of the stomach, the rules may be different. A drain is a thin tube from the wound through which blood and fluid flow into a closed bag or container.

After a first (primary) knee replacement, a drain is usually not needed. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (2022) recommends not using it routinely, because no significant improvement in the results of surgery or reduction in complications has been shown. In individual cases, the surgeon decides whether a drain is needed.

Proper leg positioning may help reduce swelling after surgery. Follow the physiotherapist's and nurse's instructions. Elevate the leg while keeping the knee straight, with support under the lower leg and heel. Do not leave a pillow directly under the bent knee for long periods, as this may make it harder to regain full extension.
When to get urgent help

After surgery, do the exercises you were given, follow the instructions about weight on the leg, and take medicines to prevent blood clots strictly as your doctor directs. Change the dressing only as the staff instruct.

If you develop new or worsening calf pain or swelling, especially on one side, seek urgent medical assessment the same day. These may be signs of a blood clot. If immediate assessment is unavailable, go to the emergency department. Contact your department or doctor the same day for spreading wound redness, pus, increasing discharge, persistent fever, chills or worsening knee pain. If you cannot reach the team or symptoms are severe, go to an emergency department (ER).
For sudden shortness of breath or chest pain, call an ambulance immediately at 101 (Magen David Adom).

Video: Hip fracture — urgent surgery
What kind of fracture this is

A hip fracture is a break in the upper part of the thigh bone (femur). A femoral neck fracture is a break in the narrow part just below the rounded head of the femur. A break immediately below the head is called a subcapital fracture.
In many older people the bones become more fragile, including because of osteoporosis. That is why a fracture can happen even in an ordinary fall.

A hip fracture usually causes pain in the groin or upper thigh. Most people cannot stand or put weight on the injured leg, and the leg may look shorter and turned outward. However, with some fractures, a person may still be able to stand or walk despite the injury.

If a hip fracture is still suspected despite a normal X-ray, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is recommended. If MRI is not available within 24 hours or cannot be performed, computed tomography (CT) may be used.

In most cases surgery is recommended. It helps reduce pain and start getting your movement back sooner. Sometimes, with a stable fracture or special medical circumstances, other treatment options are considered.

From the emergency department to the ward
The diagnosis is made in the emergency department (ER) by an examination and an X-ray. Then you are moved to the orthopedic ward, where you wait for surgery.
Until the medical team allows it, do not try to get up or walk on your own. Staff will help you change position in bed, take care of hygiene, and get ready for surgery safely.
